hr_011:n1.prompt:
You are helping me prepare to choose a work-visa strategy (H-1B, O-1, or TN) for a hire my startup cannot legally employ yet. We will work with immigration counsel through {{vendor}}. The final strategy decision remains a human step: it is a legal judgment made between me and a licensed attorney, so do not pick the visa yourself. Your job is to get me ready for that consultation.

First, ask me for anything missing:
- the candidate's citizenship
- current location and immigration status
- highest degree and field
- role, title and offered salary
- start-date deadline
- notable achievements (awards, publications, press, patents, judging, high pay)
- whether the candidate is a founder or shareholder in my company

Then:
1. Review {{vendor}}'s own materials, using your configured credentials if needed. Confirm the petition is handled by licensed immigration attorneys (named lawyers or a stated attorney-of-record model). Note what they document on:
   - H-1B, including cap-exempt routes and transfers
   - O-1A and how they assess extraordinary-ability evidence against USCIS criteria
   - TN
   - employer-side paperwork such as LCA compliance
   - founder self-petitioning (beneficial ownership, board or employer control)
2. If {{vendor}} offers a free self-serve O-1/EB-1 eligibility check, fill it out from my answers. Do not submit anything that commits me to fees or engagement without my OK.
3. Draft a one-page comparison of H-1B, O-1, and TN for this candidate. Cover apparent eligibility, timing and cap-lottery risk, evidence gaps, and the employer obligations each one creates. Label it clearly as preliminary, not legal advice.
4. Draft 8–12 questions for the attorney.
5. Help me book or request the consultation, if {{vendor}} allows it. Do not accept engagement terms on my behalf.

Done means I have three things: the candidate fact sheet, the comparison, and the question list, plus a consult booked or a clear next action. Report back with those documents, any eligibility-check result, open gaps, and links to the {{vendor}} pages you relied on.

hr_011:n2.prompt:
You are helping me assemble the evidence binder that our immigration counsel will use to support a work visa petition (H-1B, O-1, or TN) for a candidate we want to hire. If you don't already have them, ask me for: the candidate's full name, the visa category selected, the job title and duties, the employer legal name and worksite address, and where candidate-provided documents (diplomas, transcripts, resume, prior visa records) can be found or should be requested from the candidate.

Once you have these, do the following:
1. Create a checklist of required evidence tailored to the visa type: degree certificates and transcripts (with credential evaluation if foreign), employment verification letters, press mentions or publications, awards, and comparable compensation data.
2. For compensation data, pull prevailing wage benchmarks from the Department of Labor's Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OES) data and, if useful, published salary survey data from a source like the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and note the wage level that matches the role's duties and location.
3. Organize all gathered documents into a single binder (a folder or combined PDF) with a clear table of contents and a cover memo summarizing what's included and what's still missing.
4. Flag any gaps — missing transcripts, unverifiable press, no comparable wage data — as an explicit open-items list.

Done looks like: a complete, organized evidence binder (digital folder or PDF) with a table of contents, all located documents attached or linked, wage benchmark data cited with source and date, and a clear gap list for anything unresolved. Report back with the binder location/link, a summary of what's included, and the open-items list for me and counsel to review.

hr_011:n3.prompt:
You are helping me prepare a Labor Condition Application (LCA) for filing with the Department of Labor via the FLAG.gov system (https://flag.dol.gov/) as part of sponsoring a work visa (H-1B/other) for a hire. You cannot submit or sign this filing — final attestation must be done by our company's authorized signatory. Please prepare everything up to that point.

First, ask me for any missing information you need, including: the employer's legal name, FEIN, and address; the authorized signatory's name and title; the job title, SOC/O*NET occupation code, and duties; the worksite address(es); the prevailing wage determination (or ask if one has been obtained — if not, note that this must be requested first via the National Prevailing Wage Center); the offered wage rate and pay frequency; the requested employment dates; and the visa classification (H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, etc.).

Then: (1) log into or note that I need to log into the FLAG.gov system using my configured credentials; (2) draft/stage all LCA form fields (Form ETA-9035/9035E) based on the information gathered, cross-checking occupation code, wage level, and worksite details for consistency; (3) prepare the required supporting documentation checklist (prevailing wage documentation, notice of filing for posting at the worksite); (4) flag any missing or inconsistent data that would block submission; (5) compile a summary of the completed draft plus the posting/notice requirements and their timing.

Done looks like: a fully staged, error-checked LCA draft in FLAG.gov ready for review, plus a checklist of required worksite notice postings and supporting evidence, with no submission or attestation performed. Report back with the draft summary, any open questions or missing data, and the checklist — then stop for human sign-off, since the authorized signatory must review and attest under penalty of perjury before filing.

hr_011:n4.prompt:
You are helping me track the status of a Labor Condition Application (LCA) filed with the Department of Labor as part of sponsoring a work visa (H-1B, O-1, or TN track). The LCA has already been submitted via the DOL's FLAG system, and DOL has a statutory 7-business-day window to certify it. This waiting period itself remains a human step — you cannot speed up or influence DOL's internal adjudication clock.

What I need from you:
1. Ask me for: the LCA case number, the filing/submission date, and the email/login associated with our FLAG (Foreign Labor Application Gateway) account if you need context.
2. Calculate the expected certification date by counting 7 business days (excluding weekends and federal holidays) from the filing date, and give me that target date.
3. Set up a simple tracking note or checklist for me: filing date, expected certification date, case number, and a reminder to check the FLAG portal status on or after that date.
4. If asked, check the DOL FLAG portal using my configured credentials to see if the case status has changed (e.g., from 'Pending' to 'Certified' or 'Denied'/'RFI'), but only as a monitoring/verification action — do not submit anything, respond to any DOL request for information, or take corrective action on my behalf.
5. If the status shows anything other than 'Certified' (e.g., an RFI, denial, or extended review), flag this to me immediately with the exact status text so I can loop in immigration counsel.

Done looks like: you've given me the expected certification date, a tracking checklist, and either confirmation that the case is still pending (with next check-in date) or the actual certification/denial outcome if it has posted. Report back with the case number, filing date, expected date, current status as of your check, and any flags needing my attention. Remember: this DOL waiting period remains a human step — no action is required or possible from us during it.

hr_011:n5.prompt:
You are helping me prepare Form I-129 (Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker) for signature, as part of sponsoring a work visa for a hire. Signing this petition requires the petitioning employer to personally attest under penalty of perjury to its accuracy — this is a legal act that cannot be delegated to you, so you must stop before signing.

Before starting, ask me for: (1) the finalized I-129 form and all supporting evidence assembled with immigration counsel (visa category — H-1B, O-1, or TN — LCA confirmation number if applicable, job offer letter, beneficiary's credentials/evidence binder), (2) the petitioner's legal business name, FEIN, and authorized signatory's name/title, (3) any USCIS receipt or prior correspondence if this is an amendment or extension.

Your tasks: 1) Review the assembled I-129 packet for completeness — confirm all required sections are filled, the LCA is attached and matches the job details, and supporting evidence (degree certificates, resumes, employer letters, financial documents) is included per counsel's checklist. 2) Draft a summary checklist listing every document in the packet, flagging any missing items or inconsistencies (e.g., mismatched job titles, wage levels, or dates) for me or counsel to fix. 3) Prepare the signature page and any required attestations pre-filled with the authorized signatory's name, title, and date field left blank. 4) Note the correct USCIS filing address or e-filing portal and any filing fee amounts due, based on the petition type.

Once the packet is complete and verified, present me with the final checklist and signature-ready document, then stop for human sign-off. Do not sign, attest, or submit the petition yourself — physically signing and filing remains a human step that I must complete personally.

Report back with: the completeness checklist, any flagged issues, and confirmation that the packet is ready for my signature and submission.

hr_011:n6.prompt:
You are helping me prepare (not submit) the USCIS Form I-129 petition to sponsor a work visa hire, using the official process at https://www.uscis.gov/i-129. If you don't already have them from me, ask for: the beneficiary's full legal name, date of birth, and contact/passport details; the requested visa classification (H-1B, O-1, or TN) as decided with immigration counsel; the employer's legal name, FEIN, and address; the job title, duties, wage, and worksite location; the certified LCA (or LCA case number) if the classification requires it; the requested start and end dates of employment; and any supporting evidence binder documents (degree, license, prior approvals, evidence of extraordinary ability if O-1, etc.).

Please do the following:
1. Review the I-129 form instructions on the USCIS page and confirm which classification supplement and fees apply to our chosen visa type.
2. Draft a complete, accurate fill-in of Form I-129 and any required supplements using the information provided, flagging any fields where you need clarification or missing data.
3. Compile a checklist of required supporting documents (LCA, evidence binder items, fee amounts, filing location or online portal steps) and confirm each is ready or upload-ready if using the USCIS online filing portal.
4. Prepare a short cover summary listing the classification, key dates, and fee total for the authorized signer's review.
5. Do NOT sign, certify, pay, or submit the petition — actual signature and submission must be done by an authorized filer taking legal responsibility for accuracy. This remains a human step.

When done, report back: the completed draft form and supplement contents, the compiled document checklist with status, the fee summary, and a clear list of any open questions — then stop for human sign-off before anything is filed.

hr_011:n7.prompt:
You are helping me track USCIS adjudication of a work visa petition (I-129) I've already filed. The actual adjudication timeline is controlled entirely by USCIS's internal caseload and remains a human step outside anyone's control — you cannot speed it up or influence the outcome.

First, ask me for any missing details: the I-129 receipt number, the visa classification (H-1B, O-1, or TN), the service center handling the case, the filing date, and whether premium processing was requested.

Once I provide these, please:
1. Check the case status on the USCIS online case status tracker using the receipt number, and report back the current status text exactly as shown.
2. Look up the current published USCIS processing time range for this form type, classification, and service center, and compare it to our filing date to estimate a likely decision window.
3. Draft a simple tracking log (date, status checked, result) I can reuse each time I check back, and a short internal status-update note I could send to the hiring manager and candidate summarizing where things stand and the estimated timeframe.
4. If premium processing was not requested and is available for this classification, prepare a short summary of what upgrading would involve (cost, guaranteed response window) so I can decide whether to pursue it — but do not submit any request or payment on my behalf.
5. Set a reminder recommendation for when I should next check status (e.g., weekly, or at the end of the estimated processing window).

Report back with: the current case status, the estimated timeframe, the draft tracking log, the draft status-update note, and (if relevant) the premium processing summary. Do not attempt to contact USCIS, submit inquiries, or take any action on the case — adjudication remains a human step and requires waiting on USCIS's own review timeline.

hr_011:n8.prompt:
You are helping me complete the final step of sponsoring a work visa for a hire whose petition has just been approved: updating payroll and Form I-9 so they can legally start work. We use {{vendor}} as our payroll platform. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for any missing inputs: the employee's full legal name, start date, compensation details (salary, pay schedule), work location, visa type approved (H-1B, O-1, or TN), and the I-797 approval notice details (receipt number, validity dates) needed for I-9 documentation.
2. Using your configured credentials, access {{vendor}} and check whether this person already exists as a pending or prospective employee record; if not, create the new employee record with compensation and tax setup based on the details I provide.
3. Set up or trigger the self-serve onboarding flow in {{vendor}} so the employee can complete their W-4, I-9, and bank details before their start date, using their new visa status and work authorization info.
4. Confirm the employee's Form I-9 Section 1 and Section 2 fields will correctly reflect their work-authorized status (e.g., alien authorized to work, with the correct authorization expiration date pulled from the visa approval) — flag if {{vendor}} requires manual entry of this field.
5. Verify pay schedule and start date are correctly aligned so no payroll gap occurs.
6. Compile a short checklist summarizing: employee record created (yes/no), onboarding flow sent (yes/no), I-9 authorization data entered (yes/no), and any fields that could not be set automatically and need my manual review in the {{vendor}} dashboard.

Done looks like: the employee record exists in {{vendor}} with correct comp/tax setup, the onboarding flow has been sent or completed, and I-9 work authorization fields are populated or flagged for my review. Report back with the checklist above and any errors or required manual steps.
